title: Dependencies and the job graph
sub: dependsOn, CombineDependencies and a frame pipeline without needless waits
cards/0/title: dependsOn: a job waits for a job, not for the main thread
cards/0/body:
The last parameter of every Schedule is JobHandle dependsOn. A job with a dependency sits in the queue until the dependency has finished and starts right after it — on a worker thread, with no help from the main thread.

The returned handle stands for this job together with all its dependencies. In the docs’ words, completing a dependent job must first complete any job it depends on, and any jobs those depend on. So at the end of a chain one Complete() on the last handle is enough.

default(JobHandle) means “no dependency”; that is what the default parameter is.
cards/0/deep: A graph can cross a frame boundary: if the result is only needed next frame, keep the handle in a field and pass it to the first job of the next frame as dependsOn. You still need Complete() before the main thread touches the data — it is also what clears the safety system marks. And remember the manual’s advice: a job should fit within a frame.
cards/1/body:
A chain is a special case. In a real frame a job often waits for several others: that is fan-in. For it, JobHandle.CombineDependencies merges handles into one that completes when all of them have. Overloads: two handles, three, a NativeArray<JobHandle> and a NativeSlice<JobHandle>. Do not confuse it with JobHandle.CompleteAll — that one does not merge, it waits on the main thread.

The reverse is fan-out: one handle is passed to several jobs. They run in parallel if they do not conflict: the shared container is only read ([ReadOnly]), and each writes its own.

The building rule: a dependency is about data. A job depends on every unfinished job that writes what it reads, and on every job that touches what it writes.
cards/2/q: What is true about job dependencies? Pick all that apply.
cards/2/options/0: Complete() on the last handle completes the whole chain before it
cards/2/options/1: CombineDependencies takes two or three handles, or a NativeArray<JobHandle>
cards/2/options/2: A job scheduled with dependsOn blocks the main thread until the dependency finishes
cards/2/options/3: Two jobs with the same dependency that only read a shared array ([ReadOnly]) and each write their own can run in parallel
cards/2/options/4: The job system adds a dependency by itself between jobs that touch the same container
cards/2/explain: The worker threads wait; the main thread is free until Complete(). The last job’s handle pulls the whole chain along. The job system never invents dependencies: if some are missing, the safety system throws.
cards/3/title: A frame pipeline: positions → spatial hash → collisions → transforms
cards/3/body:
A typical crowd or flock frame is a chain where each link reads the previous link’s output:

  1. MoveJob integrates positions from velocities.
  2. HashJob is the spatial hash: for each agent it computes a grid cell, so neighbours are searched only nearby. In a real project this also fills a hash map or sorts by cell — parallel writing has its own lesson.
  3. CollideJob looks at neighbours by cell and writes new velocities.
  4. ApplyJob is an IJobParallelForTransform over a TransformAccessArray: it copies positions into Transforms straight from the worker threads.

The idiom: one variable h that becomes the new link’s handle at every step. Only the last one goes into a class field, and there is one Complete(), in LateUpdate.
cards/4/q: Put the links of the frame in order.
cards/4/items/1: HashJob: a grid cell for each agent
cards/4/items/2: CollideJob: neighbours by cell → new velocities
cards/4/items/3: ApplyJob: positions into Transforms via TransformAccessArray
cards/4/items/4: LateUpdate: one Complete() on the last handle
cards/4/explain: Each link reads what the previous one wrote, so each depends on the previous one. The main thread schedules the whole chain at once and waits once — at the end.
cards/5/body:
If you complete each link before scheduling the next, the main thread turns into a babysitter:

  • every Complete() blocks the main thread — in the Profiler these are WaitForJobGroupID blocks;
  • while the main thread wakes up and schedules the next job, the workers idle — gaps appear between the links;
  • the whole chain’s time comes out of the main thread’s frame instead of running alongside it.

With dependencies the whole chain is queued at once: a worker picks up the next link as soon as the previous one ends, and the main thread is free until the single Complete().

The only honest reason to wait midway is that the main thread needs a number to decide what to schedule next. Even then, think first: the decision can move into a job, and for a length known only after the previous step there is IJobParallelForDefer over a NativeList’s length.
cards/6/explain: h.Complete() in the middle of Update makes the main thread wait for MoveJob and HashJob, although CollideJob is scheduled with a dependency on h anyway. Delete the line — the dependency already guarantees the order, and there will be one Complete(), in LateUpdate.
cards/7/q: CollideJob is scheduled with a dependency on HashJob, while desired is written by SteerJob, scheduled separately. What happens in the Editor?
cards/7/options/0: An InvalidOperationException when CollideJob is scheduled: it reads desired, and SteerJob, which writes it, is not among its dependencies
cards/7/options/1: Nothing: CollideJob waits for all jobs scheduled earlier anyway
cards/7/options/2: CollideJob waits for SteerJob because both touch desired
cards/7/options/3: An exception when SteerJob is scheduled
cards/7/explain: The dependency on HashJob pulls MoveJob along, but not SteerJob — it is a separate branch. The safety system sees an unfinished writer of desired and throws. The fix is a fan-in: JobHandle.CombineDependencies(hash, steer) as CollideJob’s dependsOn.
cards/7/wrong/1: A job waits only for what is passed in dependsOn and their dependencies. Nobody waits for “everything earlier”.
cards/7/wrong/2: Dependencies are not inferred from data — you declare them, and the safety system checks whether they are enough.
cards/7/wrong/3: SteerJob is the first of the jobs touching desired to be scheduled; it has nothing to conflict with.
cards/8/q: Fix the graph: CollideJob must wait for both HashJob and SteerJob
cards/8/explain: CombineDependencies merges the two branches into one handle, and it goes into CollideJob’s dependsOn. CompleteAll would wait on the main thread, and passing only steer or only hash would lose a branch again.
cards/9/task: In Crowd three jobs are completed one by one right in Update. Turn them into a chain: hash.Schedule depends on the move handle, collide.Schedule on the hash handle; store the last handle in the handle field and wake the worker threads. Complete() goes only in LateUpdate.
cards/9/checks/0/label: hash.Schedule gets the handle from move.Schedule as a dependency
cards/9/checks/1/label: collide.Schedule gets the handle from hash.Schedule as a dependency
cards/9/checks/2/label: The handle from collide.Schedule is stored in the handle field
cards/9/checks/3/label: JobHandle.ScheduleBatchedJobs() is called after the chain is scheduled
cards/9/explain: The main thread schedules the three jobs as one batch and moves on. The workers run them back to back with no gaps, and Complete() on the last handle in LateUpdate completes the whole chain. In an interview: “I build dependencies from the data: whoever reads another job’s output depends on its writer; one Complete(), at the end.”
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “Why a dependency graph? You could just complete the jobs one by one — it’s easier to follow.”
cards/10/options/0: Every Complete() blocks the main thread and leaves the workers idle between links; with dependencies the chain runs back to back on the workers, and the main thread is free until one Complete() at the end
cards/10/options/1: Complete() may not be called more than once per frame
cards/10/options/2: Without dependencies Burst does not compile the job
cards/10/options/3: Dependencies are only needed for IJobParallelFor
cards/10/explain: The answer has two parts: main-thread time (wait once, not at every link) and worker utilization (no gaps while the main thread schedules the next job). On top of that, dependencies are what the safety system demands from jobs that share data.
cards/10/wrong/1: You may call it as often as you like — it just costs main-thread time.
cards/10/wrong/2: Burst compiles the job’s code and knows nothing about the graph.
cards/10/wrong/3: Every kind of job has dependsOn in its Schedule.
